source.name: OER Commons open containers & Docker curriculum

course.title: Docker & Containers
course.description: Package an application with everything it needs to run, then ship the exact same unit from your laptop to production without surprises. Structure adapted from open containerization curricula on OER Commons (CC BY 4.0).

questions.prompt: The main practical problem containers solve is…
options: making code run faster than native
getting the same environment on every machine
questions.explanation: Containers bundle the app with its dependencies so 'works on my machine' becomes 'works everywhere' — see 'Why containers exist'.

questions.prompt: Compared with a virtual machine, a container…
options: runs its own full guest operating system
shares the host kernel and is much lighter
requires more disk than a VM
questions.explanation: A VM virtualizes hardware and boots a full guest OS; a container shares the host kernel and isolates only the process.

questions.prompt: An image and a container relate to each other like…
questions.explanation: An image is the read-only template; a running container is a live instance created from it.

questions.prompt: Which command runs a container from an image and maps a port?
questions.explanation: docker run starts a container; -p 8080:80 publishes container port 80 on host port 8080.

questions.prompt: In a Dockerfile, the instruction that sets the starting image is…
questions.explanation: Every Dockerfile begins FROM a base image; RUN, COPY, and CMD build on top of it.

questions.prompt: To keep data after a container is deleted, you should use…
questions.explanation: A container's writable layer is discarded on removal; volumes and bind mounts persist data outside it.

questions.prompt: Docker Compose is mainly for…
options: defining and running multi-container apps from one file
questions.explanation: Compose describes several services, networks, and volumes in one YAML file and starts them together.

questions.prompt: A place you push images to so others can pull them is called a…
questions.explanation: A registry such as Docker Hub stores and distributes images by name and tag.

lessons.title: Why containers exist: VMs, and 'works on my machine'
lessons.grammar_note: A container is a process, not a tiny computer. It shares the host kernel and is isolated by kernel features (namespaces and cgroups), which is why it starts in milliseconds while a VM boots in seconds.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the problem containers solve, contrast a container with a virtual machine, and say why 'it works on my machine' happens. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, does a container boot its own operating system?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Software rarely runs alone. It depends on a specific language runtime, libraries, environment variables, and operating-system packages. When those differ between a developer's laptop and the server, the program breaks, and everyone blames the other environment — the classic 'works on my machine.' A virtual machine fixes this by shipping a whole guest operating system on top of a hypervisor; it works but is heavy, often gigabytes, and slow to start. A container takes a lighter path: it packages the application and its dependencies into an image, then runs it as an isolated process that shares the host's kernel. Isolation comes from kernel features — namespaces give the process its own view of the filesystem, network, and process list, and cgroups limit its CPU and memory. Because there is no guest OS to boot, containers are small and start almost instantly, and the same image runs identically on any machine with a container runtime.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Suppose an app needs Python 3.11 and a library that your server still has at an older version. With a VM you would provision a full guest OS and install everything by hand. With a container you write those requirements once into an image; the server pulls that image and runs the exact same bytes you tested. Compare the footprint: a minimal container image can be tens of megabytes and start in under a second, while a comparable VM image is often measured in gigabytes and takes many seconds to boot. Check what is running with 'docker ps', which lists live containers, and 'docker ps -a', which also shows stopped ones. The takeaway: a VM virtualizes hardware; a container virtualizes the operating-system environment around a single process.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In one phrase, what does a container share with its host that a VM does not? 2) Name the two kernel features that provide isolation and resource limits. 3) Why does a container usually start faster than a VM? 4) Which command lists only currently running containers? 5) True or false: a container includes a full guest operating system. Answers: 1) the host kernel. 2) namespaces (isolation) and cgroups (resource limits). 3) it has no guest OS to boot; it is just an isolated process. 4) docker ps. 5) False — it shares the host kernel and bundles only the app and its dependencies.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a container is a small virtual machine — it is an isolated process sharing the host kernel. Mistake: expecting containers to fix a real hardware or kernel incompatibility; they standardize the user-space environment, not the kernel. Exit: (a) What everyday phrase describes environment drift between machines? (b) What does a container share with the host? Answers: 'works on my machine'; the host kernel.

lessons.title: Images vs containers and the Docker model
lessons.grammar_note: One image, many containers. The image is read-only; each running container adds a thin writable layer on top that is discarded when the container is removed.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish an image from a container, describe how a name and tag identify an image, and sketch how the Docker client, daemon, and registry cooperate. Warm-up: if an image is like a class, what is a running container?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An image is a read-only template: a stack of filesystem layers plus metadata that says how to start the program. A container is a running instance created from an image, with a thin writable layer added on top. From one image you can start many containers, just as one class produces many objects. Images are named as repository plus tag, for example 'nginx:1.27' or 'myapp:latest'; the tag is a human label, not a guarantee of uniqueness, while a content digest identifies exact bytes. Three parts make up the everyday model. The Docker client is the 'docker' command you type. The daemon is the background service that actually builds images and runs containers. A registry, such as Docker Hub, stores images so they can be shared. When you run 'docker run nginx', the client asks the daemon to run it; if the image is not present locally, the daemon pulls it from the registry first.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: List local images with 'docker images' and pull one explicitly with 'docker pull nginx:1.27'. Start two containers from that single image: 'docker run -d --name web1 nginx:1.27' and 'docker run -d --name web2 nginx:1.27'. Both share the same read-only layers; each has its own writable layer and its own name. Inspect details with 'docker inspect web1'. Remove a container with 'docker rm web1' and its writable layer disappears, but the image remains, ready to spawn more containers. If you never specify a tag, Docker assumes ':latest', which is simply the default label — not necessarily the newest version — so pinning an explicit tag like ':1.27' makes builds reproducible.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which one is read-only, the image or the container? 2) In 'redis:7.2', which part is the tag? 3) Which component actually runs containers: the client or the daemon? 4) What does 'docker images' show? 5) If you omit a tag, which tag does Docker use? Answers: 1) the image. 2) 7.2. 3) the daemon. 4) the images stored locally. 5) latest, the default label.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating ':latest' as 'the newest release' — it is just the default tag and can point at anything. Mistake: expecting a removed container's writable data to survive; only the image persists. Exit: (a) One image can produce how many containers? (b) Name the background service that builds and runs. Answers: many; the Docker daemon.

lessons.title: Running containers: docker run, ports, and env vars
lessons.grammar_note: In -p HOST:CONTAINER the host port comes first. -p 8080:80 means 'reach container port 80 by visiting host port 8080' — mixing up the order is the most common beginner bug.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Start, name, and stop containers; publish ports; pass environment variables; and open a shell inside a running container. Warm-up: in -p 8080:80, which number is the host port?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The 'docker run' command creates and starts a container from an image. Useful flags shape how it runs. '-d' runs it detached in the background; without it, the container's output stays attached to your terminal. '--name web' gives it a readable name instead of a random one. '-p 8080:80' publishes a port, mapping host port 8080 to container port 80 so the outside world can reach the service. '-e KEY=value' sets an environment variable inside the container, the standard way to pass configuration such as credentials or feature flags. '--rm' deletes the container automatically when it exits, handy for short-lived tasks. Once a container runs you manage it by name: 'docker stop web' sends a graceful shutdown, 'docker start web' resumes it, 'docker logs web' prints its output, and 'docker exec -it web sh' opens an interactive shell inside it.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Run a web server in the background and reach it at localhost:8080: 'docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx'. Pass configuration to a database via environment variables: 'docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret -p 5432:5432 postgres:16'. Watch what a container prints: 'docker logs -f web' follows the log stream. Step inside to look around: 'docker exec -it web sh', then type 'ls' and 'exit' to leave without stopping the container. Run a throwaway one-off that cleans up after itself: 'docker run --rm alpine echo hello' prints hello and removes the container. Finally stop and delete: 'docker stop web' then 'docker rm web'.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which flag runs a container in the background? 2) Write the flag that maps host port 3000 to container port 3000. 3) How do you set an environment variable named DEBUG to true? 4) Which command opens an interactive shell in a running container named api? 5) What does --rm do? Answers: 1) -d. 2) -p 3000:3000. 3) -e DEBUG=true. 4) docker exec -it api sh. 5) removes the container automatically when it exits.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reversing the port order and writing -p 80:8080 when you meant -p 8080:80. Mistake: baking secrets into an image instead of passing them at run time with -e or a secrets mechanism. Exit: (a) Which flag names a container? (b) In -p 8080:80, what is port 80? Answers: --name; the container's internal port.

lessons.title: Building images with a Dockerfile
lessons.grammar_note: CMD sets the default command run when the container starts; RUN executes a command while building the image. Build-time versus run-time is the distinction to hold onto.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read and write a basic Dockerfile, understand the common instructions, and build an image with a tag. Warm-up: which instruction must appear first in almost every Dockerfile?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A Dockerfile is a plain-text recipe for building an image, one instruction per line. FROM chooses the base image to start from. WORKDIR sets the working directory for later steps. COPY brings files from your project into the image. RUN executes a command during the build, typically to install dependencies, and the result becomes part of the image. ENV sets an environment variable baked into the image. EXPOSE documents which port the app listens on. CMD gives the default command that runs when a container starts from the image. The key contrast: RUN happens once while building the image, whereas CMD happens each time you run a container. You turn a Dockerfile into an image with 'docker build', tagging it so you can refer to it later.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A Dockerfile for a small Node.js app might read: FROM node:20-alpine / WORKDIR /app / COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ / RUN npm ci / COPY . . / ENV NODE_ENV=production / EXPOSE 3000 / CMD ["node", "server.js"]. Build it from the directory that holds the Dockerfile: 'docker build -t myapp:1.0 .' — the trailing dot is the build context, the folder Docker sends to the daemon. Then run it: 'docker run -d -p 3000:3000 myapp:1.0'. Notice the two COPY steps: copying the dependency manifest and installing before copying the rest of the source lets Docker reuse the install step when only your code changes, which you will explore next in caching. Verify the new image exists with 'docker images'.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which instruction sets the base image? 2) Which instruction runs at build time, RUN or CMD? 3) What does the trailing dot mean in 'docker build -t app .'? 4) Write the flag that tags an image as web:2.0 during a build. 5) Which instruction documents the port the app listens on? Answers: 1) FROM. 2) RUN. 3) it is the build context, the current directory sent to the daemon. 4) -t web:2.0. 5) EXPOSE.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing RUN (build time) with CMD (container start time). Mistake: forgetting the build context dot, or building from the wrong directory so COPY cannot find files. Exit: (a) Which instruction sets the default start command? (b) What does 'docker build -t name:tag .' produce? Answers: CMD; a tagged image.

questions.prompt: The clearest difference between a container and a VM is that a container…
questions.explanation: Containers share the host kernel and isolate a process; VMs boot a full guest OS — see 'Why containers exist'.

questions.prompt: One image can be used to start…
questions.explanation: An image is a read-only template; many containers can be instantiated from it.

questions.prompt: In 'docker run -p 8080:80 nginx', host port 8080 maps to…
questions.explanation: The form is -p HOST:CONTAINER, so 8080 on the host reaches port 80 inside the container.

questions.prompt: To pass a configuration value into a container at run time, use…
questions.explanation: -e sets an environment variable inside the container.

questions.prompt: Which Dockerfile instruction sets the base image?
questions.explanation: FROM chooses the starting image and normally appears first.

questions.prompt: RUN differs from CMD because RUN executes…
questions.explanation: RUN runs at build time and bakes its result into the image; CMD runs when a container starts.

lessons.title: Layers, caching, and image size
lessons.grammar_note: Order Dockerfile steps from least-changing to most-changing. Dependencies change rarely, source changes constantly — copy and install dependencies before copying source so the cache survives edits.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how image layers and the build cache work, order Dockerfile steps for fast rebuilds, and shrink images. Warm-up: if you edit one source file, should the dependency-install step have to run again?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a layer, a saved snapshot of the filesystem changes it made. Layers stack to form the image, and they are cached. When you rebuild, Docker walks the instructions and reuses a cached layer as long as that instruction and everything before it are unchanged. The moment one step changes, that layer and every layer after it must be rebuilt — the cache is invalidated from that point down. This is why step order matters: copy your dependency manifest and install dependencies early, then copy your fast-changing source code later, so routine code edits do not trigger a full reinstall. Image size matters too, because smaller images pull and start faster. Choose slim base images such as an Alpine or slim variant, combine related RUN commands to avoid extra layers, and use a .dockerignore file so junk like node_modules or .git is never sent into the build.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Consider a Dockerfile that copies everything first, then installs: FROM node:20-alpine / WORKDIR /app / COPY . . / RUN npm ci. Editing a single source file changes the COPY layer, so the expensive 'npm ci' reruns every time. Reorder it: FROM node:20-alpine / WORKDIR /app / COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ / RUN npm ci / COPY . . Now a code edit only invalidates the final COPY; the install layer stays cached and rebuilds finish in seconds. Add a .dockerignore containing lines like 'node_modules', '.git', and 'Dockerfile' to keep the build context small. Inspect the layer history and sizes with 'docker history myapp:1.0', and compare total sizes with 'docker images'. Switching a base image from a full 'node:20' to 'node:20-alpine' often cuts hundreds of megabytes.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does each Dockerfile instruction create? 2) If an early layer changes, what happens to the layers after it? 3) Why copy package.json and install before copying the rest of the source? 4) Name a file that keeps unwanted paths out of the build context. 5) Name one way to reduce image size. Answers: 1) a layer (a cached filesystem snapshot). 2) they are invalidated and rebuilt. 3) so code edits do not invalidate the cached dependency install. 4) .dockerignore. 5) use a slim or Alpine base image, or combine RUN steps, or ignore junk files.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: copying all source before installing dependencies, which destroys the cache on every edit. Mistake: shipping a heavy base image and the whole build context, bloating the image. Exit: (a) What invalidates the build cache from a given step downward? (b) Which file excludes paths from the build context? Answers: a change to that step (or any earlier one); .dockerignore.

lessons.title: Persisting data: volumes and bind mounts
lessons.grammar_note: A named volume is managed by Docker and best for real data (databases); a bind mount maps a host folder into the container and is best for live-editing source during development.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why container data is ephemeral, and use named volumes and bind mounts to persist or share files. Warm-up: if you delete a database container with no volume, what happens to its data?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A container's writable layer lives and dies with the container; remove the container and that data is gone. To keep data you store it outside the container. Docker offers two main mechanisms. A named volume is storage that Docker creates and manages in its own area; you refer to it by name, and it survives container removal — ideal for databases and other durable state. A bind mount maps a specific folder on the host directly into the container; whatever is in that host folder appears inside, and edits flow both ways — ideal for developing, since you can change source on your machine and see it live in the container. You attach either with the -v flag on 'docker run', or in Compose. Volumes are portable and managed; bind mounts tie you to a host path but give you a direct window into real files.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Create and use a named volume so a database keeps its data across restarts: 'docker volume create pgdata', then 'docker run -d --name db -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:16'. Delete and recreate the container with the same -v and the data is still there, because the volume outlived the container. List volumes with 'docker volume ls' and inspect one with 'docker volume inspect pgdata'. Use a bind mount for live development, mapping your project folder into the container: 'docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 -v $(pwd)/site:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro nginx'. The ':ro' makes it read-only inside the container. Edit a file in ./site on your host and refresh the browser to see it immediately, with no rebuild.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Why is a container's own writable layer not a safe place for a database? 2) Which option is managed by Docker: a named volume or a bind mount? 3) Which is best for live-editing source during development? 4) Write the flag that mounts a volume named data at /app/data. 5) What does :ro add to a mount? Answers: 1) it is deleted with the container, so data is lost. 2) a named volume. 3) a bind mount. 4) -v data:/app/data. 5) it makes the mount read-only inside the container.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming data survives container removal without a volume — it does not. Mistake: using a bind mount for production database storage, tying durable data to a fragile host path. Exit: (a) Which mechanism does Docker manage for you? (b) What is lost when you remove a container that had no volume? Answers: the named volume; its writable-layer data.

lessons.title: Container networking
lessons.grammar_note: On a user-defined bridge network, containers reach each other by container name, which Docker resolves through built-in DNS. 'localhost' inside a container means that container itself, not the host or a sibling.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how containers talk to each other and to the outside world, create a user-defined network, and connect containers by name. Warm-up: inside a container, does 'localhost' mean the host machine?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: By default Docker gives each container a private IP on a bridge network and lets it reach the internet, but to expose a service to your host you must publish a port with -p. Containers on the same user-defined bridge network can talk to each other directly, and Docker provides DNS so they can use each other's container names as hostnames — an app container can connect to 'db:5432' simply because a container is named db on the shared network. This name-based discovery is why you rarely hardcode container IP addresses. A crucial subtlety: 'localhost' inside a container refers to that container alone, never the host or a sibling container, so services find each other by container name over a shared network, not by localhost. Common network drivers include bridge (the default, for single-host container-to-container traffic), host (the container shares the host's network stack directly), and none (no networking).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Create a network and put two containers on it so they can find each other by name: 'docker network create appnet'. Start a database: 'docker run -d --name db --network appnet -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:16'. Start an app on the same network that connects to the database by its name: 'docker run -d --name api --network appnet -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://db:5432/app -p 3000:3000 myapp:1.0'. Here the api reaches the database at host 'db' — no IP address needed — because both share appnet and Docker resolves the name. From the host you still reach the api only through the published port 3000. Inspect a network and see which containers are attached with 'docker network inspect appnet', and list networks with 'docker network ls'.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which flag exposes a container port to the host? 2) On a shared user-defined network, how do containers address each other? 3) Inside a container, what does 'localhost' refer to? 4) Which command creates a network named appnet? 5) Name the default network driver for container-to-container traffic on one host. Answers: 1) -p (publish). 2) by container name, resolved through Docker's DNS. 3) that same container itself. 4) docker network create appnet. 5) bridge.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: telling one container to reach another at 'localhost' — it must use the sibling's container name on a shared network. Mistake: hardcoding container IP addresses, which change; use names instead. Exit: (a) How does an app container reach a container named db? (b) What must you add to reach a container's service from the host? Answers: by the hostname 'db' on a shared network; a published port with -p.

questions.prompt: Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a…
questions.explanation: Instructions build cached filesystem layers that stack into the image — see 'Layers, caching, and image size'.

questions.prompt: You copy package.json and install dependencies before copying source so that…
options: code edits do not invalidate the cached install
questions.explanation: Ordering least-changing steps first preserves the cache when only source changes.

questions.prompt: To keep a database's data after its container is removed, use…
questions.explanation: A named volume is managed by Docker and outlives the container.

questions.prompt: A bind mount is most appropriate for…
questions.explanation: A bind mount maps a host folder in, so edits appear instantly inside the container.

questions.prompt: On a shared user-defined network, one container reaches another by…
options: its container name via Docker DNS
questions.explanation: Docker resolves container names to addresses on the shared network.

questions.prompt: Inside a container, 'localhost' refers to…
questions.explanation: localhost is the container itself, which is why siblings are addressed by name.

lessons.title: Multi-container apps with Docker Compose
lessons.grammar_note: Compose gives every service a network automatically, and the service name becomes its hostname. Define 'db' and 'web' and the web service can reach the database at host 'db' with no extra configuration.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe what Docker Compose is for, read a compose file, and bring a multi-service app up and down with one command. Warm-up: how many YAML files does Compose use to describe several services?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Real applications are rarely one container. A typical stack has a web app, a database, and maybe a cache, each in its own container, wired together. Running and reconnecting all of them by hand with long 'docker run' commands is tedious and error-prone. Docker Compose solves this: you describe the whole application in one YAML file, 'compose.yaml', listing each service with its image or build, ports, environment variables, volumes, and dependencies. Then 'docker compose up' starts everything, creates a shared network so the services can reach each other by name, and 'docker compose down' stops and removes it all. Compose is the standard way to run multi-container apps on a single machine, both for local development and for simple deployments. It turns a fragile sequence of manual commands into one readable, version-controlled file.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A compose.yaml for a web app plus a database might read: services: / web: / build: . / ports: / - "3000:3000" / environment: / - DATABASE_URL=postgres://db:5432/app / depends_on: / - db / db: / image: postgres:16 / environment: / - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret / volumes: / - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data / volumes: / pgdata:. Start the whole stack in the background with 'docker compose up -d'; Compose builds the web image, pulls postgres, creates a network, and starts both. The web service reaches the database at host 'db' because that is its service name. Watch output with 'docker compose logs -f', list services with 'docker compose ps', and tear everything down with 'docker compose down'. Add '-v' to that last command to also delete named volumes when you truly want a clean slate.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What problem does Compose solve compared with many docker run commands? 2) What is the usual filename for a Compose file? 3) Which command starts the whole stack in the background? 4) In the example, at what hostname does 'web' reach the database? 5) Which command stops and removes the stack? Answers: 1) it defines and runs a multi-container app from one file instead of fragile manual commands. 2) compose.yaml. 3) docker compose up -d. 4) db (the service name). 5) docker compose down.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: expecting depends_on to wait until a database is fully ready — it only controls start order, so apps should retry their connection. Mistake: running 'docker compose down -v' by habit and wiping volumes you meant to keep. Exit: (a) One Compose file describes how many services? (b) How does a service address another service? Answers: as many as you list; by its service name as a hostname.

lessons.title: Registries and sharing images
lessons.grammar_note: A full image reference is registry/repository:tag. Docker Hub is the default registry, so 'nginx:1.27' expands to 'docker.io/library/nginx:1.27'. Other registries must be named explicitly in the reference.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what a registry is, log in, tag an image for a repository, and push and pull it. Warm-up: what is the default registry when you type 'docker pull nginx'?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A registry is a service that stores and distributes images, letting you share a build so a teammate or a server can pull the exact same bytes. Docker Hub is the default public registry; others include GitHub Container Registry and the registries run by cloud providers. An image reference has three parts: the registry host, the repository name, and the tag, written registry/repository:tag. When the registry is omitted, Docker assumes Docker Hub. To publish, you authenticate with 'docker login', tag your local image with the target repository name, and push it. Anyone with access can then pull it by that reference. Tags are how you version and channel releases — for example a specific version like 1.0.3 alongside a moving label like latest — and because tags can be moved, teams often also pin by the immutable content digest for reproducible deployments.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Suppose your Docker Hub username is jordan. Build and tag an image for your repository: 'docker build -t jordan/myapp:1.0 .'. Authenticate: 'docker login'. Push it so others can pull: 'docker push jordan/myapp:1.0'. On another machine, retrieve exactly that image: 'docker pull jordan/myapp:1.0' and run it. To retag an existing local image for a different registry, use 'docker tag myapp:1.0 ghcr.io/jordan/myapp:1.0' and then push to that host. Give the same build two tags — a version and latest — by tagging twice before pushing both: 'docker tag jordan/myapp:1.0 jordan/myapp:latest'. For a deployment you never want to drift, reference the digest, which looks like 'jordan/myapp@sha256:...', so you always get identical bytes regardless of where tags later point.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is a registry for? 2) In 'jordan/myapp:1.0', which part is the tag? 3) Which command uploads an image to a registry? 4) What registry does Docker assume when none is given? 5) Why might a team deploy by digest instead of by tag? Answers: 1) to store and distribute images so they can be shared and pulled. 2) 1.0. 3) docker push. 4) Docker Hub. 5) a digest is immutable, so it guarantees identical bytes even if tags move.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: trying to push without first logging in or without tagging the image to your repository name. Mistake: trusting 'latest' for production, since it can be moved to point at a different build. Exit: (a) Which command downloads an image from a registry? (b) What are the three parts of an image reference? Answers: docker pull; registry, repository, and tag.

lessons.title: Orchestration intro and capstone: containerize a small app
lessons.grammar_note: Compose runs many containers on one machine; an orchestrator like Kubernetes runs many containers across many machines and keeps them running. Reach for orchestration when a single host and manual restarts are no longer enough.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why orchestration and Kubernetes exist, describe what they add beyond Compose, and complete a capstone that containerizes a small two-service app end to end. Warm-up: if one server is not enough and containers must self-heal across a cluster, what tool category do you need?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Compose is perfect for one machine, but production often needs more: many servers, automatic restarts when a container crashes, scaling to more copies under load, rolling updates with no downtime, and load balancing across instances. Doing all that by hand does not scale, which is why orchestration exists. An orchestrator manages containers across a cluster of machines: you declare the desired state — say, 'run five copies of this image, keep them healthy' — and the orchestrator continuously works to match reality to that declaration, rescheduling containers when a node fails. Kubernetes is the most widely used orchestrator. It introduces its own vocabulary — a Pod wraps one or more containers, a Deployment keeps a desired number of replicas running, and a Service gives them a stable network address — but the core idea is simple: declarative, self-healing, scalable container management. You do not need Kubernetes to start; most projects begin with a Dockerfile and Compose and adopt orchestration only when scale demands it.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Capstone. Containerize a small app that has a web service and a Postgres database. Step 1, write the Dockerfile for the web app: FROM node:20-alpine / WORKDIR /app / COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ / RUN npm ci / COPY . . / ENV NODE_ENV=production / EXPOSE 3000 / CMD ["node", "server.js"]. Step 2, add a .dockerignore with lines 'node_modules', '.git', and 'npm-debug.log' to keep the build small. Step 3, write compose.yaml: services: / web: / build: . / ports: / - "3000:3000" / environment: / - DATABASE_URL=postgres://db:5432/app / depends_on: / - db / db: / image: postgres:16 / environment: / - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret / volumes: / - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data / volumes: / pgdata:. Step 4, bring it up: 'docker compose up -d --build'. Step 5, verify: 'docker compose ps' shows both services, 'docker compose logs -f web' shows the app booting, and visiting localhost:3000 reaches it. Step 6, tear down cleanly with 'docker compose down', keeping the pgdata volume for next time.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name two things an orchestrator does that plain Compose on one machine does not. 2) In Kubernetes, what keeps a desired number of replicas running? 3) What does a Kubernetes Service provide? 4) In the capstone, which command builds and starts the whole stack? 5) Which capstone file keeps node_modules and .git out of the image? Answers: 1) any two of: run containers across many machines, restart or reschedule failed containers, scale replicas, roll out updates without downtime, load balance. 2) a Deployment. 3) a stable network address for a set of Pods. 4) docker compose up -d --build. 5) .dockerignore.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reaching for Kubernetes on day one when a Dockerfile plus Compose would do — added complexity without payoff. Mistake: in the capstone, forgetting the volume so the database resets on every 'down'. Exit: (a) What is the one-line reason orchestration exists? (b) Which command tears the capstone stack down? Answers: to run and keep containers healthy and scaled across many machines; docker compose down.

lessons.title: Final quiz: containers end to end

questions.prompt: The essential difference between a container and a VM is that a container…
options: shares the host kernel and isolates a process
questions.explanation: Containers share the host kernel; VMs virtualize hardware and boot a full guest OS.

questions.prompt: An image is to a container as…
options: a file is to a folder
a class is to an instance
a tag is to a digest
a port is to a volume
questions.explanation: The image is the read-only template; a container is a running instance of it.

questions.prompt: 'docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx' does which of these?
options: runs nginx in the background, reachable on host port 8080
questions.explanation: -d detaches, --name names it, and -p 8080:80 publishes container port 80 on host 8080.

questions.prompt: In a Dockerfile, RUN versus CMD is best summarized as…
options: RUN at container start, CMD at build
RUN at build time, CMD at container start
questions.explanation: RUN executes during the build and bakes into the image; CMD is the default command when a container starts.

questions.prompt: Copying package.json and running the install before copying source mainly improves…
options: build cache reuse on code edits
questions.explanation: Least-changing steps first keep the cached dependency layer valid when only source changes.

questions.prompt: To persist a database across container removal, the right tool is…
questions.explanation: A named volume is managed by Docker and outlives the container.

questions.prompt: On a shared user-defined network, an app container reaches a container named db via…
questions.explanation: Docker resolves container names on the shared network, so 'db' works as a hostname.

questions.prompt: Docker Compose is best described as a tool to…
options: define and run multi-container apps from one file
questions.explanation: Compose declares several services in one YAML file and runs them together with a shared network.

questions.prompt: To share an image so a server can pull it, you…
options: docker login, tag, then docker push
docker network create, then docker ps
questions.explanation: Authenticate, tag to the target repository, and push to a registry; others then pull it.

questions.prompt: The core reason Kubernetes and other orchestrators exist is to…
options: run and self-heal containers, scaled across many machines
questions.explanation: Orchestrators keep declared numbers of containers healthy and scaled across a cluster.

questions.prompt: Inside a running container, 'localhost' refers to…
questions.explanation: localhost is the container itself, which is why siblings are addressed by name over a shared network.

questions.prompt: When no registry is named in 'docker pull nginx:1.27', Docker uses…
questions.explanation: Docker Hub is the default registry, so the reference expands to docker.io/library/nginx:1.27.
